cover.alt: A young adult places a book beside morning coffee and fruit to begin a small reading habit.

blocks.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Small habits feel hard at first, but they get easier. You will see why a clear cue and one tiny action, done again and again, can turn a new behavior into something automatic in daily life.

blocks.title: Before You Read
blocks.intro: Think about your own day before reading.

items.prompt: What is one small thing you do every morning without thinking?
items.explanation: Try: brushing teeth, making coffee, checking the phone.

items.prompt: What usually reminds you to do it?
items.explanation: A time, a place, or another action can be the reminder.

blocks.title: A Cue Starts the Habit
paragraphs: A cue is a small signal that tells your brain, "Time to do this now." It can be a time, a place, or an action you already do. Researchers Lally and colleagues at University College London studied 96 people who tried to build a new daily habit. Each person chose a clear cue, like "after breakfast," and then did one small action, like eating a piece of fruit. When the cue was the same every day, the action became automatic faster. A weak or changing cue made the habit much harder to keep.

items.prompt: In the University College London study, what did each person choose to help start the new habit?
choices: A long list of goals for the year
A friend to do the habit for them
A new phone app every week
items.explanation:
Each person picked one steady cue and then did one small action right after it.

What cue in your day could you use to start a new small habit?

blocks.title: Repetition Makes It Easy
paragraphs: Doing the same small action after the same cue, day after day, is called repetition. In the same study, the action felt more automatic each time people did it. At first, the line on their chart went up quickly: the second and third days felt much easier than the first. Later, the line got flatter, but the habit kept growing. On average, people needed about 66 days before the action felt truly automatic. Some habits, like drinking a glass of water after breakfast, became automatic in around 20 days. Harder habits, like doing 50 sit-ups after coffee, took much longer.

items.prompt: About how many days did people need, on average, before the new action felt automatic?
items.explanation:
The study found an average of about 66 days, though simple habits were faster and harder ones took longer.

Which of your habits took a long time to feel easy, and which felt easy quickly?

blocks.title: Keep the Action Tiny
paragraphs: A tiny action is easier to repeat than a big one. Imagine two people who want to read more. Maria puts one book next to her coffee cup every night. Her cue is "after I pour my coffee in the morning," and her action is "read one page." Tom tells himself he will read for one hour every day. On busy days, Maria still reads her one page, so her habit grows. Tom often skips his hour, so his cue and action never connect. Small actions win because they still happen when you are tired, late, or not in the mood.

items.prompt: Why does Maria's habit grow while Tom's does not?
items.answer: Her action is tiny, so she can do it even on busy days
choices: Her action is tiny, so she can do it even on busy days
She has more free time than Tom
She reads only very short books
items.explanation:
One page after coffee is small enough to repeat every day, so the cue and action stay connected.

What is one habit you could shrink to a very tiny version this week?

blocks.title: Final Reflection
paragraphs: Small habits become easier when a clear cue meets one tiny action, and both are repeated in the same order every day. The cue tells your brain when to start. The tiny action is small enough to survive busy or tired days. Over weeks, often around 66 days, the action stops feeling like a decision and starts feeling normal. You do not need strong willpower; you need the same simple pattern, done again and again.

rows.meaning: a small signal that starts a habit
rows.example: Pouring coffee is my cue to read one page.

rows.meaning: doing the same thing again and again
rows.example: Repetition made the action feel automatic.
After weeks, brushing teeth feels automatic.

rows.meaning: a very small step that is easy to do
rows.example: Reading one page is a tiny action.

rows.meaning: something you do regularly, often without deciding
rows.example: Drinking water after breakfast is a good habit.
